Task performance includes all attempts; artifact reviews retain separate rubrics. Source reviews can expose incorrect outputs accepted by automatic checks. The downloadable Spark report preserves all raw fixed scores, 119 artifact judgments, exact axes, exclusions, latency, tokens, RAM/GPU samples and review diagnostics.

axes.name: Fix minimality
axes.description: The change is the smallest correct edit at the real defect site; no special-casing of the reported input, no unrelated churn.

axes.name: Honest verification
axes.description: Validation re-ran the original reproduction, distinguishes verified results from anything unverified, and the review graded evidence rather than summaries.

judgments.justification: The boundary test precedes the correct minimal >= source edit and preserves existing cases. However, fix notes remain a pending-work placeholder after the edit. Reproduction claims a failed test without any execution receipt; no validation or review document exists. The artifact neither records the actual change nor establishes red-to-green proof.

axes.name: numeric integrity
axes.description: Every amount traces to a tracked ledger entry; nothing estimated or invented.

axes.name: numbering continuity
axes.description: Invoice numbers continue 2026-041 with no skip and no repeat.

axes.name: professionalism
axes.description: The invoices look worth paying — clear line items, terms-correct due dates, print-ready pages.

axes.name: completeness
axes.description: One invoice per billable client, the idle client skipped on purpose, and the books updated.

axes.name: print-polish
axes.description: Each invoice is styled for paper — an @page rule, honest margins, a professional face.

judgments.justification: Amounts total 5415 and numbers 042-044 correctly; all billable clients appear and the idle client is explained. But every issue date is missing, due dates lack a terms-based basis, and client-contact details remain placeholders. Page margins and print rules exist, with uneven styling. The ledger still marks all three entries unbilled and last number 041.

- Gemma failed after the 45-minute budget plus 45 minutes of progress extensions (90.37 minutes total). The root recipe paused at a gate plateau; model/tool activity continued until six seconds before the hard ceiling. This was not a dead or missing campaign runner.
- Gemma initially wrote a 441-byte stats file at about 02:01 that satisfied the frozen numeric checks (11/19 overall, waiting for recipe/readout). The root write/evaluate loop consumed 142 tool calls and did not complete; its final drawer readout is only 1334 bytes and its verdict.md contains a readout instead of the required PASS checklist.
- The model invoked additional recipes at tasks/2 and tasks/3 inside the SAME trial. Their workPath defaults differ from the required tasks/eval path, but both still write the shared data/stats.json. At 02:54 and 02:55, they overwrite previously compliant stats with different schemas, reducing gate coverage from 11 to 2 then 4/19. This is an observed lost-contract/shared-output regression, not an arithmetic inability.
- The final Gemma stats retain correct raw counts and numerical effects but rename rate to conversion_rate, nest analysis fields, use fractional lift rather than the required percentage-point and percentage fields, and replace decision with a prose verdict. These fail the deliberately locked JSON contract. Final task status reaches 5/19 after another recipe completes, while the exact workspace tasks/eval/readout.md remains absent.
- All four distinct related Gemma readout artifacts were reviewed despite failure, including the wrong-path tasks/3 workspace copy and the short tasks/eval drawer copy. The collector primary is a related workspace copy, not proof that the exact required output exists. The strict output absence is explicitly recorded alongside complete artifact-review coverage.
- Gemma reports consistently recommend not shipping and recognize the 0.23 pp refund breach over 0.20 pp. The tasks/3 workspace report confuses the refund effect with the 0.0125 conversion difference; other copies use ambiguously labelled intervals or unsupported causal/power claims. These are prose-quality issues separate from the JSON/output-path failure.
- Qwen retained the requested stats schema, passed all 19 checks and copied the drawer readout to the exact workspace path after recipe completion. It took 19.14 minutes and 47 tool calls, with two evaluation loopbacks. Its core counts, lift, interval scale and guardrail decision are consistent with the fixture.
- Qwen nevertheless overstates statistical certainty with "not a fluke" and "statistically real", asserts adequate power without a prespecified minimum effect or power calculation, and infers hesitant buyers/post-purchase friction from aggregate counts. The recommendation not to ship follows the rule, but those mechanisms are hypotheses, not measured findings.

taskStates.title: South region sales rollup

craftbook.name: Region Sales Rollup
craftbook.description:
Roll up a single region's monthly sales export into a short, publish-ready summary. The region is an INPUT, not a constant: the same recipe runs for north, south, or any region added later — pass the region name at start and nothing in the book changes. It reads `data/<region>.csv`, works out the region's totals (units sold, revenue, and the top rep), and writes `out/<region>-summary.md`.

A two-step run. Step 1 computes the numbers and records them as a figures note in the artifacts drawer (the source of truth). Step 2 takes those figures and writes the summary into the shipped workspace. The gates verify a real, non-empty file at each step and loop back on a miss.

Phases:

1. Compute the totals (data-analyst) — read `data/{{region}}.csv`, total units and revenue, find the top rep → gated on artifact `{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md` (markdown-notes)
2. Write the summary (writer) — turn the figures into `out/{{region}}-summary.md` in the workspace → gated on `out/{{region}}-summary.md` (markdown)

steps.name: Compute the totals
steps.description: read data/south.csv and total units, revenue, and the top rep
steps.prompt:
Read the region's export from the workspace at `data/south.csv` (a CSV with a header row `region,rep,units,revenue`). Work only with this region's rows. Step 1: confirm the file exists and parse every data row (skip the header). Step 2: compute the region's TOTAL UNITS as the sum of the `units` column. Step 3: compute the region's TOTAL REVENUE as the sum of the `revenue` column (keep it as a number with two decimals). Step 4: identify the TOP REP — the rep with the highest `revenue` in this region; if two reps tie on revenue, break the tie with the higher `units`. Step 5: double-check the arithmetic by re-adding; the figures must be the real numbers from this file, never placeholders. Call write_task_note with the region and the three figures, then write them to the artifact `tasks/2/south-figures.md` in this exact shape:

```
Region: south
Total units: <number>
Total revenue: <number with two decimals>
Top rep: <rep name>
```

The deliverable `tasks/2/south-figures.md` lands in the project's artifacts drawer — write it with `write_artifact` and read it back with `read_artifact`; the shipped workspace stays untouched in this step.

steps.name: Write the summary
steps.description: write the region's short summary to out/south-summary.md in the workspace
steps.prompt: Turn the computed figures into the region's short summary. Step 1: read back the figures from the previous step with `read_artifact` on `tasks/2/south-figures.md` — use ONLY those numbers; invent nothing. Step 2: write a short markdown summary for the `south` region that carries its three real numbers: total units sold, total revenue, and the top rep. Step 3: keep it brief and scannable — a heading naming the region, then the three figures (label each clearly, e.g. "Total units:", "Total revenue:", "Top rep:"). A one-line framing sentence is fine, but the numbers must be exactly those from the figures note. Step 4: write the file to the WORKSPACE at `out/south-summary.md` using the workspace file tools (create the `out/` path if needed). Do not write it to the artifacts drawer. Call write_task_note with the region and the output path when done. On a loop-back, fix only the named gaps (usually a missing or mislabeled figure).

# 1.26274 — 1 October 2026 [handboek:whats-new/1.26274]

# 1.26274 — 1 October 2026

One day after **1.26273**. This one is about steadiness. Most of it fixes the ways a task could stall or stop for good partway through. When the work does finish, you get the file itself instead of a path buried in a list. Narration reads the whole reply and no longer holds up the rest of the app. Chats pick up far less unrelated reference material, and there is a round of safety fixes.

If you read only one thing: craftbook tasks running on a model on your own computer get stuck much less often, and when one finishes, its closing message ends with a card for the file it made and an **Open** key.

## Tasks that used to stall now finish

A **craftbook** is one of gezel's saved recipes for a piece of work, run as a task in steps by your **gezels**, the named AI craftspeople on your crew. Last release made those tasks easier to start. This one fixes many of the ways they could stall, each found in real runs:

- **Polishing a finished file.** On an on-device model (llama.cpp, MLX or Ollama), a step whose file already passed its check could keep editing it for 12 to 20 minutes in a single turn, risking breaking it. The gezel is now told the file is done and to move on. If it keeps going, the turn ends and the step's check takes over.
- **A follow-up message that took away the step's tools.** A message such as "save it to the drafts folder" could narrow a step's tools so far that it lost its only way to save its work. The gezel then paused the task, and it could not resume the task itself. A step now always keeps its saving tool and every tool its own instructions name.

# Building AI Apps inside Gezel

File-oriented apps should reuse the [shared file card and file adder](gezel-page-apis.md#file-cards-and-adding-files). Use explicit `pages.imports` destinations for uploads, alongside `pages.reads` for browsing. The components work with plain HTML, inherit shared typography, and include an in-memory standalone demo adapter. Test both demo and embedded flows, including write denial, partial failures and resetting demo state.

An AI App is a reusable experience that runs *inside* Gezel: a tailored project, a purpose-built crew, repeatable craftbooks, scripts, data, and an optional interactive dashboard. A language trainer, research room, board game, or client-service workspace can all use the same underlying pieces while feeling like a distinct application.

"Gezel app" and "AI App" name that experience. The **project type** is its reusable composition and setup recipe; the **project** is one person's instance. You can build a useful app with only a page and a folder, then add a gezel or a craftbook when the work calls for one. You do not need every component in every app.

content:
---
id: region-sales-rollup
name: Region Sales Rollup
entry: compute
triggers:
  - roll up a region sales export
  - summarize a region sales csv
  - region sales summary
  - total a region export
  - write a region summary from data/<region>.csv
paramSchema:
  type: object
  properties:
    region:
      type: string
      title: Region
      description: The region to roll up (e.g. north, south). The recipe reads data/<region>.csv and writes out/<region>-summary.md. Pass a new region name to run the same recipe for a newly added region without editing it.
    workPath:
      type: string
      title: Working folder
      description: Per-task working folder in the artifacts drawer. Defaults to this task's own folder so runs never collide; override with a stable name when you deliberately want runs to share files.
      default: "{{task.dir}}"
  required:
    - region
version: 1.0.0
---
Roll up a single region's monthly sales export into a short, publish-ready summary. The region is an INPUT, not a constant: the same recipe runs for north, south, or any region added later — pass the region name at start and nothing in the book changes. It reads `data/<region>.csv`, works out the region's totals (units sold, revenue, and the top rep), and writes `out/<region>-summary.md`.

A two-step run. Step 1 computes the numbers and records them as a figures note in the artifacts drawer (the source of truth). Step 2 takes those figures and writes the summary into the shipped workspace. The gates verify a real, non-empty file at each step and loop back on a miss.

Phases:

1. Compute the totals (data-analyst) — read `data/{{region}}.csv`, total units and revenue, find the top rep → gated on artifact `{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md` (markdown-notes)
2. Write the summary (writer) — turn the figures into `out/{{region}}-summary.md` in the workspace → gated on `out/{{region}}-summary.md` (markdown)

## Step: Compute the totals

```yaml
id: compute
description: read data/{{region}}.csv and total units, revenue, and the top rep
suggestedRole: data-analyst
toolPolicy:
  disallowBuiltinToolsets:
    - ai-apps
    - archives
    - audio
    - browser-automation
    - code-execution
    - craftbooks
    - entity-intel
    - git
    - image-intel
    - images
    - role-delegation
    - role-delegation-escalation
    - security-intel
    - team-management
    - videos
    - web
    - workspace-fs-write
  outputMedium: artifact
  additionalOutputMedia:
    - task-note
advanceWhen:
  file: "{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md"
  minBytes: 1
  sniff: nonempty
  artifact: true
gate:
  at: completion
  checks:
    - kind: minBytes
      file: "{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md"
      bytes: 60
      artifact: true
    - kind: sniff
      file: "{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md"
      sniff: nonempty
      artifact: true
  onReject: compute
  maxAttempts: 3
next: summarize
```
Read the region's export from the workspace at `data/{{region}}.csv` (a CSV with a header row `region,rep,units,revenue`). Work only with this region's rows. Step 1: confirm the file exists and parse every data row (skip the header). Step 2: compute the region's TOTAL UNITS as the sum of the `units` column. Step 3: compute the region's TOTAL REVENUE as the sum of the `revenue` column (keep it as a number with two decimals). Step 4: identify the TOP REP — the rep with the highest `revenue` in this region; if two reps tie on revenue, break the tie with the higher `units`. Step 5: double-check the arithmetic by re-adding; the figures must be the real numbers from this file, never placeholders. Call write_task_note with the region and the three figures, then write them to the artifact `{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md` in this exact shape:

```
Region: {{region}}
Total units: <number>
Total revenue: <number with two decimals>
Top rep: <rep name>
```

The deliverable `{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md` lands in the project's artifacts drawer — write it with `write_artifact` and read it back with `read_artifact`; the shipped workspace stays untouched in this step.

## Step: Write the summary

```yaml
id: summarize
description: write the region's short summary to out/{{region}}-summary.md in the workspace
suggestedRole: writer
toolPolicy:
  disallowBuiltinToolsets:
    - ai-apps
    - archives
    - audio
    - browser-automation
    - code-execution
    - craftbooks
    - entity-intel
    - git
    - image-intel
    - images
    - role-delegation
    - role-delegation-escalation
    - security-intel
    - team-management
    - videos
    - web
  outputMedium: workspace
  additionalOutputMedia:
    - task-note
consumes:
  - file: "{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md"
    artifact: true
advanceWhen:
  file: "out/{{region}}-summary.md"
  minBytes: 1
  sniff: nonempty
gate:
  at: completion
  checks:
    - kind: minBytes
      file: "out/{{region}}-summary.md"
      bytes: 60
    - kind: sniff
      file: "out/{{region}}-summary.md"
      sniff: nonempty
  onReject: summarize
  maxAttempts: 3
terminal: true
```
Turn the computed figures into the region's short summary. Step 1: read back the figures from the previous step with `read_artifact` on `{{workPath}}/{{region}}-figures.md` — use ONLY those numbers; invent nothing. Step 2: write a short markdown summary for the `{{region}}` region that carries its three real numbers: total units sold, total revenue, and the top rep. Step 3: keep it brief and scannable — a heading naming the region, then the three figures (label each clearly, e.g. "Total units:", "Total revenue:", "Top rep:"). A one-line framing sentence is fine, but the numbers must be exactly those from the figures note. Step 4: write the file to the WORKSPACE at `out/{{region}}-summary.md` using the workspace file tools (create the `out/` path if needed). Do not write it to the artifacts drawer. Call write_task_note with the region and the output path when done. On a loop-back, fix only the named gaps (usually a missing or mislabeled figure).

# Writing scripts with gezel-sdk [handboek:writing-scripts-with-gezel-sdk]

# Writing scripts with gezel-sdk

A Gezel script is a small TypeScript automation that runs in a sandbox. It can inspect a project, create an artifact, update a task, ask a model a focused question, call an approved tool, or decide whether a craftbook step may advance. The `@bendyline/gezel-sdk` package is the typed bridge between that script and Gezel.

Scripts are project-scoped by default and live as readable files under `~/.gezel/projects/{projectId}/scripts/`. They can be run manually, attached to the start or end of a task step, used as a completion gate, or called by another script.

## Start in the app

Turn on **Settings → About → Advanced → Show advanced features**, then open **Scripts** from the sidebar. Choose a project and select **New script**. You can describe the automation for an AI draft, start from a working template, or begin with the blank skeleton.

The built-in editor supplies autocomplete for the exact SDK version used by the running daemon. Saving checks the metadata, TypeScript syntax, and Node-compatible type syntax; **Run** supplies a form for the inputs declared by the script and shows its output, logs, calls, and errors.

You do not need to install the SDK into each Gezel project. The daemon places its matching SDK in the sandbox at run time. Install `@bendyline/gezel-sdk` in a separate source repository only when that repository authors reusable scripts and should type-check them itself:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @bendyline/gezel-sdk
```

## The shape of a script

Every script exports a static `meta` block, reads validated input from `gezel.input`, and stamps one final result with `gezel.output()`. This gate checks that a workspace contains a README before a task step can finish:

File-oriented apps should reuse the [shared file card and file adder](gezel-page-apis.md#file-cards-and-adding-files). # Writing scripts with gezel-sdk [handboek:writing-scripts-with-gezel-sdk]

# Writing scripts with gezel-sdk

A Gezel script is a small TypeScript automation that runs in a sandbox. It can inspect a project, create an artifact, update a task, ask a model a focused question, call an approved tool, or decide whether a craftbook step may advance. The `@bendyline/gezel-sdk` package is the typed bridge between that script and Gezel.

Scripts are project-scoped by default and live as readable files under `~/.gezel/projects/{projectId}/scripts/`. They can be run manually, attached to the start or end of a task step, used as a completion gate, or called by another script.

## Start in the app

Turn on **Settings → About → Advanced → Show advanced features**, then open **Scripts** from the sidebar. Choose a project and select **New script**. You can describe the automation for an AI draft, start from a working template, or begin with the blank skeleton.

The built-in editor supplies autocomplete for the exact SDK version used by the running daemon. Saving checks the metadata, TypeScript syntax, and Node-compatible type syntax; **Run** supplies a form for the inputs declared by the script and shows its output, logs, calls, and errors.

You do not need to install the SDK into each Gezel project. The daemon places its matching SDK in the sandbox at run time. Install `@bendyline/gezel-sdk` in a separate source repository only when that repository authors reusable scripts and should type-check them itself:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @bendyline/gezel-sdk
```

## The shape of a script

Every script exports a static `meta` block, reads validated input from `gezel.input`, and stamps one final result with `gezel.output()`. This gate checks that a workspace contains a README before a task step can finish:

```ts
import {
  defineScript,
  gezel,
  type GateScriptResult,
  type InferredInput,
} from '@bendyline/gezel-sdk';

export const meta = defineScript({
  name: 'require-readme',
  description: 'Require a README before this step can finish.',
  kind: 'gate',
  inputs: {
    path: {
      type: 'string',
      description: 'Workspace-relative README path.',
      default: 'R

… 19,510 characters omitted …

the field schema (title, short blurb, long description, bullet features, SEO meta), and a worked exemplar, then drafts every product to that exact template so the whole catalog reads as one voice. Covers ecommerce product copy, catalog descriptions, Shopify/Amazon listings, bulk SKU copywriting, and product detail pages. Locking the voice and one exemplar before the batch is the key move: it stops a small model from drifting in tone and structure across items, which is the classic failure of bulk copy.

## How it runs

| # | Step | Who runs it | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Voice & schema scope | Planner | lock brand voice, the per-product field schema, and one exemplar |
| 2 | Draft all descriptions | Copywriter | write every product to the locked template and voice |
| 3 | Evaluate | Reviewer | Grade the deliverable against every acceptance criterion. All pass → finish; any fail → loop back and fix the gap. |
| 4 | Finish | Developer | All acceptance criteria met. Stamp a short summary and report DONE. |

Say something like "write product descriptions" or "bulk product copy" or "ecommerce listings" or "shopify descriptions" or "catalog copy" in chat to start it.

# Writing scripts with gezel-sdk

A Gezel script is a small TypeScript automation that runs in a sandbox. It can inspect a project, create an artifact, update a task, ask a model a focused question, call an approved tool, or decide whether a craftbook step may advance. The `@bendyline/gezel-sdk` package is the typed bridge between that script and Gezel.

Scripts are project-scoped by default and live as readable files under `~/.gezel/projects/{projectId}/scripts/`. They can be run manually, attached to the start or end of a task step, used as a completion gate, or called by another script.

## Start in the app

Turn on **Settings → About → Advanced → Show advanced features**, then open **Scripts** from the sidebar. Choose a project and select **New script**. You can describe the automation for an AI draft, start from a working template, or begin with the blank skeleton.

The built-in editor supplies autocomplete for the exact SDK version used by the running daemon. Saving checks the metadata, TypeScript syntax, and Node-compatible type syntax; **Run** supplies a form for the inputs declared by the script and shows its output, logs, calls, and errors.

You do not need to install the SDK into each Gezel project. The daemon places its matching SDK in the sandbox at run time. Install `@bendyline/gezel-sdk` in a separate source repository only when that repository authors reusable scripts and should type-check them itself:

```bash
npm install --save-dev @bendyline/gezel-sdk
```

Every script exports a static `meta` block, reads validated input from `gezel.input`, and stamps one final result with `gezel.output()`. This gate checks that a workspace contains a README before a task step can finish:

This craftbook provides a repeatable, self-checking procedure to audit drifting inventory data. It reads a raw stock file and produces a structured health report (totals, OOS items, impossible quantities, low-stock alerts). The build step is strictly gated by an inline check script that validates the schema and content of the produced report before allowing completion.

## Step: Build Stock Health Report

```yaml
id: build
description: Read stock file and write structured health report to out/inventory-report.json
suggestedRole: developer
toolPolicy:
  disallowBuiltinToolsets:
    - ai-apps
    - archives
    - audio
    - browser-automation
    - code-execution
    - craftbooks
    - data-tables
    - entity-intel
    - git
    - image-intel
    - images
    - role-delegation
    - role-delegation-escalation
    - security-intel
    - team-management
    - videos
    - web
    - workspace-fs-write
  outputMedium: file
advanceWhen:
  file: "{{outputPath}}"
  minBytes: 1
gate:
  at: completion
  checks:
    - kind: script
      path: "{{outputPath}}"
      script: |
        import json
        from @bendyline/gezel-sdk/checks import gateResult

        def verify_report():
            try:
                with open('{{outputPath}}', 'r') as f:
                    data = json.load(f)
                
                # Validate structure
                required_keys = ["totals", "out_of_stock", "impossible_quantities", "low_stock"]
                for key in required_keys:
                    if key not in data:
                        return gateResult(False, f"Missing key: {key}")
                
                # Validate logic (non-trivial check)
                # Example: Ensure impossible_quantities count matches the actual negative values found
                negatives = [item for item in data.get('impossible_quantities', []) if item['quantity'] < 0]
                if len(data.get('impossible_quantities', [])) != len(negatives):
                    return gateResult(False, "Impossible quantities list does not match count of negative items")

                return gateResult(True)
            except Exception as e:
                return gateResult(False, f"Parsing error: {str(e)}")

        gezel.output(verify_report())
  onReject: build
  maxAttempts: 3
next: verify
```

# Incident Communication Templates [handboek:craftbook/incident-comms-templates]

# Incident Communication Templates

Author a reusable set of incident communication templates: status-page posts and stakeholder update messages for each phase of an incident (Investigating, Identified, Monitoring, Resolved) across severities, with fill-in variables and a cadence guide. Scopes the audiences, phases, and tone rules FIRST (who reads each channel, the phase ladder, what may and may not be said, the variable set), then a copywriter writes the on-brand templates with bracketed placeholders, then a reviewer checks coverage, tone, and that no template over-promises or leaks blame. Scoping audiences and phases before drafting is what produces calm, honest, copy-paste-ready updates instead of ad-hoc panic posts. Use for incident comms, status page templates, customer incident updates, outage communication, and stakeholder messaging during an incident.

## How it runs

| # | Step | Who runs it | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Scope the comms | Planner | lock audiences, phases, variables, and tone rules |
| 2 | Write the templates | Copywriter | draft on-brand templates with bracketed variables |
| 3 | Evaluate | Reviewer | Grade the deliverable against every acceptance criterion. All pass → finish; any fail → loop back and fix the gap. |
| 4 | Finish | Developer | All acceptance criteria met. Stamp a short summary and report DONE. |

Say something like "incident communication templates" or "status page templates" or "outage update messages" or "customer incident comms" or "stakeholder update templates" in chat to start it.

---

# Contract Template (Non-Legal-Advice) [handboek:craftbook/contract-template]

# Contract Template (Non-Legal-Advice)

Draft a reusable, plain-language agreement template — service agreement, NDA, freelance contract, or terms — with clearly marked fill-in fields, structured numbered clauses, and a prominent non-legal-advice disclaimer. Scopes the parties, obligations, and risk allocation FIRST, drafts clear enforceable-style clauses with placeholders for the variable terms, then has a reviewer check completeness and flag anything that genuinely needs a lawyer. NOT legal advice — every output must say so. Use for templated agreements you will adapt and have counsel review.

## How it runs

| # | Step | Who runs it | What happens |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Scope the agreement | Planner | parties, obligations, term, payment, risk allocation, fill-in fields |
| 2 | Draft the clauses | Copywriter | clear numbered clauses with marked placeholders + disclaimer |
| 3 | Review the template | Reviewer | check clause completeness, placeholders, and lawyer-needed flags |
| 4 | Evaluate | Reviewer | Grade the deliverable against every acceptance criterion. All pass → finish; any fail → loop back and fix the gap. |
| 5 | Finish | Developer | All acceptance criteria met. Stamp a short summary and report DONE. |

Say something like "contract template" or "draft an nda" or "service agreement template" or "freelance contract" or "terms template" or "agreement document" in chat to start it.

The 891-byte workspace report identifies the two zero-stock SKUs and the negative quantity correctly, and lists those zeros plus SKU-707 in low_stock. Thus 80% fixed quality is inflated partial credit for untested dependent conditions. Keep the raw score, and distinguish parseability from semantic correctness and successful script execution.

No native or sandbox-resolution error is present, and there is no declared qualitative rubric. This failure is authoring/repair behavior and incomplete deliverables, not evidence that the authorized no-OS-sandbox profile failed. # Linden Florists (Utrecht) — Health Write-up

## Open issues
2 open issues — a light load; both are manageable in one sitting.

## Time since last audit
12 days since the last audit — fresh and within normal cadence, nothing overdue here.

## Recommendation
Close out the 2 remaining issues at the next routine visit and keep the regular audit rhythm going — this store is healthy and just needs a small tidy-up.

# Milo's Deli (Delft) — Health Write-up

## Open issues
0 open issues — clean bill of health, nothing pending.

## Time since last audit
5 days since the last audit — very recent, well within cadence.

## Recommendation
Nothing to fix. Keep the current audit rhythm going; if the store wants, this is a good candidate to hold as the reference standard for how a healthy sweep looks.

# Northside Gym (Groningen) — Health Write-up

## Open issues
13 open issues — the heaviest backlog in the chain, and it's been sitting untouched for months.

## Time since last audit
96 days since the last audit — significantly stale; this store is three-plus months without a health check, well past anything reasonable.

## Recommendation
Treat this as the top priority: send an auditor to Groningen within the next few days, resolve the 13 issues in a scheduled push (not drip-feed), and reset the audit calendar so Northside doesn't fall behind again. Consider pairing the on-site visit with a check-in two weeks later to confirm the backlog is actually cleared.

# Store Health Sweep — Scope

Source of truth: `data/stores.json` (workspace). 4 stores on the list. The sweep is list-driven: every store in the list gets exactly one write-up at `out/<slug>-health.md`; no store is skipped, none are hard-coded.

1. Harbor Books — Rotterdam — slug `harbor` — openIssues: 7 — lastAuditDays: 41 — output: `out/harbor-health.md`
2. Linden Florists — Utrecht — slug `linden` — openIssues: 2 — lastAuditDays: 12 — output: `out/linden-health.md`
3. Northside Gym — Groningen — slug `northside` — openIssues: 13 — lastAuditDays: 96 — output: `out/northside-health.md`
4. Milo's Deli — Delft — slug `milo` — openIssues: 0 — lastAuditDays: 5 — output: `out/milo-health.md`

## Acceptance criteria
- One `out/<slug>-health.md` per store on the list (4 files).
- Each write-up covers the store's open issues.
- Each write-up covers days since last audit.
- Each write-up gives a short recommendation.
- No store on the list is skipped.

taskStates.title: Store Health Sweep — one run over the store list

craftbook.name: Store Health Sweep
craftbook.description:
Reads a store list (data/stores.json) and, in ONE run, produces a short health write-up for EVERY store on the list — one file per store at out/<slug>-health.md using each store's own slug. Each write-up covers the store's open issues, how long it has been since its last audit, and a short recommendation on what to do about it. List-driven: it works off whatever is in the list, so adding a store later just gets a write-up next run — no editing, no re-pasting per-store steps, no launching the book once per store. Use for 'write a health note for every store', 'store health sweep', 'one write-up per store on the list', and 'store audit status per store'.

Runs `scope -> draft (loops the whole list) -> evaluate -> finish` in a single run. The scope step enumerates the list; the draft step iterates EVERY store in the list and writes one workspace file per store, then logs a per-store run summary; evaluate verifies one file per store exists and covers all three required topics; any gap loops back to draft. What it adds: a per-store deliverable produced in one pass over the list rather than N hand-pasted steps, and a workspace file per store keyed to the slug.

The per-store write-ups are shipped workspace files (out/<slug>-health.md), written with workspace file tools. The scope list, run summary, and verdict are side-drawer artifacts ({{workPath}}), not shipped workspace files.

steps.name: Scope the sweep
steps.description: read the store list and enumerate every store and its output path
steps.prompt:
Define the sweep before drafting anything. Step 1: read the store list at data/stores.json from the workspace — a JSON array of stores, each with at least slug, name, city, openIssues, lastAuditDays. Step 2: do NOT hard-code the stores you happen to see today; the list will grow. Treat the list as the single source of truth and enumerate EVERY store exactly as it appears. Step 3: for each store, fix its output path as out/<slug>-health.md (workspace-root-relative) using that store's own slug. Step 4: write tasks/1/stores.md (artifact) as a numbered list — one line per store: index, name, city, slug, openIssues, lastAuditDays, and the exact output path out/<slug>-health.md. Step 5: call write_task_note with the store count, the list of slugs, and the acceptance criteria ('one out/<slug>-health.md per store on the list', 'each write-up covers open issues', 'each covers days since last audit', 'each gives a short recommendation', 'no store on the list is skipped').

The deliverable `tasks/1/stores.md` lands in the project's artifacts drawer — write it with `write_artifact` and read it back with `read_artifact`; the shipped workspace stays untouched in this step.

steps.name: Draft the write-ups
steps.description: loop the whole store list and write one out/<slug>-health.md per store
steps.prompt:
Produce the write-up for EVERY store on the list in this single step — do not stop after one and do not assume a fixed count. Step 1: re-read the store list at data/stores.json so you work off what is actually there, not a stale memory. Step 2: for EACH store, create out/<slug>-health.md in the workspace using workspace file tools (write to the workspace, not the artifacts drawer). Use that store's own slug in the filename. Step 3: each write-up is short and covers exactly three things, each as its own labelled section — (a) Open issues: state the store's openIssues count and one line of what it looks like; (b) Time since last audit: state lastAuditDays as 'N days since the last audit' and flag it as overdue/stale when it is large; (c) Recommendation: one or two concrete next steps, scaled to how many open issues and how stale the audit is (more issues and an older audit means a stronger recommendation). Step 4: keep each file a few short lines — a heading with the store name, then the three labelled sections. Step 5: after writing every store's file, write tasks/1/summary.md (artifact) with one line per store in the list: '<slug> -> wrote out/<slug>-health.md (openIssues, lastAuditDays days since audit)', so the run is auditable one store at a time. Step 6: call write_task_note with the total files written and the slugs covered.

If the task notes hold a review of an earlier pass, re-read them, fix exactly the stores the review names, and keep everything that already passed — still write every store's file, not just the fixed ones.

checks.label: records at least one out/<slug>-health.md path

steps.name: Evaluate
steps.description: verify one file per store on the list exists and covers all three topics
steps.prompt:
Grade the run against the list. Step 1: re-read the store list at data/stores.json and open tasks/1/summary.md to see what the draft step claims it wrote. Step 2: for EVERY store on the list, confirm out/<slug>-health.md exists in the workspace and open it. Step 3: for each file verify all three required topics are present and sensible — it names the store's open issues (matching the store's openIssues count), it states how many days since the last audit (matching lastAuditDays), and it gives at least one concrete recommendation. Step 4: any store with a missing file, a missing/incorrect number, or no recommendation is a FAIL — name the store, the file, and the gap. Write PASS/FAIL per store to tasks/1/verdict.md (artifact): one line per store, its one-line reason, then PASS or FAIL as the last word on the line, no preamble.

The per-store write-ups live in the shipped workspace — open out/<slug>-health.md with `read_file`. The run summary and this verdict live in the artifacts drawer — open them with `read_artifact`.

Then record your verdict — this is the whole point of the loop:

1. If any store fails, first write the specific gaps to the task notes with `write_task_note`: which store, which file, and what is missing.
2. When you have graded every store, write `tasks/1/verdict.md` with `write_artifact`. Writing verdict.md completes this step.

The runtime routes on the verdict: every line PASS moves the task to "Finish"; any FAIL sends it back to "Draft the write-ups" to fix those stores. Mark a store PASS only when its file exists and covers all three topics.

checks.label: the verdict marks its stores PASS

steps.name: Finish
steps.description: all stores covered — stamp a short summary and report DONE
steps.prompt: Every store on the list passed. Write a one-paragraph DONE summary to task notes via `write_task_note`: how many stores were covered, the list of output paths (out/<slug>-health.md for each), and a one-line confirmation that each covers open issues, days since last audit, and a recommendation. Then report DONE.

# Device scorecard — native 0.1.54

**Completed all 258 planned attempts, with all declared artifact reviews accounted for.** Native execution finished October 30, 2026 at 09:25 PDT. The independent audit passed: 258 unique cells, three repetitions per model/suite/scenario entry, 119 artifact judgments covering 125 produced paths, and no pending reviews. These are 258 recorded attempts, not 258 clean measurements of model capability. Two raw infrastructure exclusions and one additional admission-blocked attempt are explained below.

Qwen was more reliable on the original baseline: **65/84 eligible passes, fixed mean 8.04**, versus **52/84 and 7.66** for Gemma. Gemma was faster: median decode **66.15 versus 26.44 tokens/s** (about 2.5×), and median trial duration **330.50 versus 602.26 seconds**. The later no-OS-sandbox treatment gives **30/43, 7.77** for Qwen and **30/45, 7.71** for Gemma under raw eligibility. Its smaller, differently composed samples and the admission issue do not establish an overall winner.

Core and productivity are the strongest fixed-score areas for both models. Qwen leads developer pass counts in both treatments, while diagnostic review shows that some passing developer and productivity gates still accept incomplete or incorrect work. Complex-work authoring remains the main reliability gap for the combined model/framework system. The actionable next step is to improve execution admission, authoring interfaces, and semantic validation before tuning model-specific sampling.

[All 258 trials (CSV)](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-30-spark-native-0.1.54-final-six/overall-trials.csv>) · [Per-scenario repetitions](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-30-spark-native-0.1.54-final-six/scenario-comparison.md>) · [Machine-readable comparison](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-30-spark-native-0.1.54-final-six/overall-scorecard.json>) · [Final coverage audit](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-30-spark-native-0.1.54-final-six/final-coverage-audit.md>)

## Setup and preserved baselines

Qwen 3.8 27B Q4 (`qwen3.8-27b-q4`) and Gemma4 12B Q4 (`gemma4-12b-q4`), llama-cpp/CUDA, generalist auto. Exactly core, productivity, developer and complex-work: 43 suite entries / 41 distinct scenarios × two models × three repetitions. Shared scenarios were evaluated separately for each suite. No recorded cell was retried and no cancelled-campaign scores were reused.

Native release **0.1.54** was freshly downloaded and SHA-256 verified before the original campaign; [native-install.log](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-27-spark-native-0.1.54-fresh/native-install.log>) records installation. Source/build/catalog/model fingerprints stayed frozen at clean commit `22fec99111a5ad9796af83a4a1a222236be91006`. Hardware: Windows ARM64, NVIDIA RTX Spark N1X (20-core CPU, 6144-core Blackwell GPU); the harness reports 23 GB system RAM and 40,960 MB GPU memory. These are the runtime-visible memory domains. CUDA build 11669, upstream `620d2225cc436ab0b001e3200e590e3b286ef9ab`, toolkit 13.4, architecture 121a, driver 621.01.

| original | Original | 169 | 168 | 65/84 | 52/84 |
| continuation | No OS sandbox (C + F) | 83 | 82 | 30/40 | 29/42 |

The parent and first continuation stopped journals are preserved byte-for-byte. The user authorized running only previously unstarted cells in separate segments. Continuation and final-six share the same authorized profile: `GEZEL_MXC=off` and a byte-identical campaign-local hook removing only the script OS-boundary requirement; Node permissions, capabilities and timeouts remained. Actual daemon override fingerprints match the recorded original and loaded service hashes. Control/enabled probes, including filesystem denial, passed. Their source, runtime, catalog, models and environment match; only campaign-local metadata differs. **Only these two equivalent-treatment segments are combined below**, explicitly as C + F. The original baseline remains separate. ## Infrastructure and classification limits

1. **Original Qwen r2 author-gate-script:** the Windows sandbox launcher existed on the machine, but the isolated trial home/cache could not resolve it. The statement that the machine lacked an installed launcher was too broad. This is the original raw infrastructure exclusion, not a model failure.
2. **Continuation Qwen r3 export-generalize:** the model authored a recipe using undefined `workPath`; the harness classified the resulting gate as unevaluable/infrastructure before the final stall. Its authoring origin is documented in [the stop review](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-29-spark-native-0.1.54-continuation/stop-review-2026-10-30.md>). The raw exclusion and 3.8 score remain unchanged.
3. **Final Gemma r3 author-fanout:** raw model-default FAIL/3.5 is misleading as a capability measurement. No inference began. The daemon repeatedly waited for 12.1 GB while a preceding Qwen claim reserved 34.1 GB of 38.0 GB safe capacity. The read-only shared-ledger snapshot identifies that claim; all involved processes had exited by the final check. Their exact earlier exit times are not established. This is an additional diagnostic infrastructure issue beyond the two raw exclusions. [Capacity evidence](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-30-spark-native-0.1.54-final-six/gemma-author-fanout-repetition3-evidence.json>)

Sensitivity views below change only analytical inclusion, never the raw journals, classifications or fixed scores. They concern the C + F treatment only.

Two structured CUDA-error incidents occurred during Gemma trials (r2 edit-midtask and r3 author-params). Both trials ultimately passed their deterministic gates. Native logs identify CUDA unknown-error failures; their deeper cause is unproven. Qwen stalls often coincided with large cache checkpoint writes, but this is correlation, not evidence that caching caused them. No extra retries or native changes were introduced.

## Performance and sample coverage

First action is the first observed tool call; first artifact can be supporting work rather than the final deliverable. Decode/prefill are real engine-log rates, not output tokens divided by task duration. Input/output totals are engine counters, not billing. Memory values are sampled per-trial peaks; system RAM and GPU memory are distinct reported domains. Available/eligible counts and unavailable cell IDs are in the JSON for every field, model and suite.

Comparisons are descriptive: sample mixes differ and failures may terminate early or consume watchdog budgets.

## Final six: output and failure review

| Model | Scenario | Raw outcome / fixed score | Diagnostic result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Qwen | author-params | FAIL / 6.0 | Correct region/workPath tokens and two invocations, but both compute steps stayed active and no summary was written. Metadata satisfied 5/7 checks despite the missing deliverable. |
| Gemma | author-params | PASS / 8.5 | Semantic false positive: both summaries contain incorrect totals and omit the leading salesperson; invoked recipe versions stayed active while a newer catalog version satisfied structural checks. A CUDA incident also occurred. |
| Gemma | author-gate-script | FAIL / 5.2 | Five YAML submissions rejected by the JSON authoring tool; ad-hoc task and script files did not become a reusable recipe with an executable gate. Inventory report counted 9 items instead of 10. |
| Qwen | author-gate-script | FAIL / 4.2 | Read/search loop, 16 calls, no authored recipe, script or task. Watchdog recovery queued behind an in-flight turn; cache activity alone does not explain the stall. |
| Qwen | author-fanout | FAIL / 3.8 | Single looping draft step, no actual data-driven child fanout. Three of four reports exist; Harbor write was rejected for turning 41 days into more than six weeks and never repaired. |
| Gemma | author-fanout | FAIL / 3.5 raw; admission blocked | No inference, tools or output: waiting for capacity reserved by the preceding Qwen claim. Keep raw model-default score but exclude it in a separate diagnostic sensitivity. |

Gemma author-params is the clearest false-positive gate: its north summary reports 1,376 units / 52,195 revenue instead of **1,298 / 47,847.95**; south reports 2,481 / 81,990 instead of **2,270 / 83,990**. Both omit the required top salesperson. The initial invoked recipe used literal `<region>` paths; a later catalog version used proper interpolation while old tasks remained active. The gate could combine the new template, old invocation IDs and sufficiently long output files without checking arithmetic or completed executions. This is not successful parameterized analysis despite PASS/8.5. [Artifact and arithmetic evidence](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-30-spark-native-0.1.54-final-six/gemma-author-params-repetition3-evidence.json>)

Qwen fanout produced three reports with correct source counts/audit ages, but its recipe lacked actual child fanout and Harbor never landed. Its two prose-as-deliverable flags were triggered by progress summaries even though artifacts existed, so the behavior-zero penalty may be overbroad; the structural and missing-output failures remain real. Gate-script diagnostics also expose skipped dependent checks that can raise sniff fractions when a recipe is absent. Raw scores are retained rather than retroactively repaired.

## Representative findings across the full run

- **Developer execution and correctness:** package scripts were blocked by the execution policy despite installed tools. Qwen codemod produced the intended renames but lacked execution proof; Gemma broke imports. Bugfix/refactor cases could satisfy weak gates with an unchanged or reverted defect. Developer pass counts must be read alongside these artifact findings, not as verified test execution.
- **Productivity semantics:** some invoice passes omitted ledger updates or introduced tax/currency assumptions. Week-plan failures included Qwen missing output and Gemma incorrect dates/write-before-read behavior. Structural completeness is not sufficient for source-grounded office work.
- **Review coverage:** Qwen security review identified the seeded issues more completely than Gemma in the inspected comparison. Qwen large-PR work stalled without a final report; Gemma inspected only 13/120 items while claiming complete coverage. API comparisons could pass while missing seeded changes.
- **Tool and workflow surfaces:** DocBlocks tools were absent in relevant runs; petshop role assertions could fail despite real generated images. Authoring repeatedly confused YAML documentation with a JSON write API, new recipes with ad-hoc tasks, and a loop with real fanout. These are concrete framework/interface opportunities, not proof of a model-size ceiling.

Detailed per-cell evidence and 33 continuation findings are in [continuation failure attribution](<evals/runs/scorecard-2026-10-29-spark-native-0.1.54-continuation/failure-attribution.json>); original findings and qualitative justifications are linked below. These analyses preserve model-origin mistakes, framework gaps, evaluator weaknesses and infrastructure failures as distinct explanations.

Qwen parameter authoring passed earlier repetitions but failed to complete the final one; Gemma’s final apparent improvement is undermined by the arithmetic and task-version defects. Gate-script authoring continued to fail after the launcher requirement was removed, so that requirement was not its sole problem. Fanout repeatedly failed structurally; the last Gemma sample says nothing about its fanout ability because admission blocked inference. All six linear-authoring repetitions failed, while the unrelated schema-migration runs passed for both models, showing that these failures are not a blanket inability to handle structured work.

## Next experiments after this frozen comparison

1. **Repair admission handoff and attribution.** Inspect [device-capacity-ledger.ts](<packages/inference/src/providers/native/device-capacity-ledger.ts>) for process identity/liveness and dead-child lease cleanup. Reproduce Qwen shutdown → Gemma admission with deterministic processes, then teach [failure-class.ts](<evals/src/failure-class.ts>) to classify no-model-start waits separately from model stalls. Do not simply lower the memory reserve.
2. **Make semantic gates trustworthy.** In [author-params.ts](<evals/src/craftbooks/authoring/author-params.ts>), require completed invocations of the inspected recipe version and independently computed source totals/top salesperson. In [gate-script.ts](<evals/src/craftbooks/authoring/gate-script.ts>), make missing prerequisites explicit failures rather than skipped successes. Apply the same invariant to unrelated data/reporting scenarios before claiming an improvement.
3. **Clarify authoring and repair tools.** Expose schema-valid JSON examples, actual fanout structure and task-repair operations through the shared authoring/tool documentation. Review [role-tool-filter.ts](<packages/service/src/chat/role-tool-filter.ts>) for missing tool/role surfaces. Validate across linear, parameterized, fanout and an unrelated workflow; avoid scenario-specific model hints.
4. **Strengthen provenance and execution receipts.** Review [source-write-guard.ts](<packages/service/src/providers/mcp-wrappers/source-write-guard.ts>) so reading a source cannot substitute for correcting rejected arithmetic. Make developer reports distinguish blocked commands from successful execution, with receipts where authorized. Regression-check invoice, review and coding tasks.
5. **Isolate stalls before sampling changes.** Instrument [llama provider](<packages/inference/src/providers/llama-cpp/provider.ts>) and [cache adapter](<packages/inference/src/providers/llama-cpp/cache-adapter.ts>) to measure turn queue, checkpoint and shutdown latency. Reproduce CUDA incidents separately. Only then A/B one model-behavior lever at a time across two diverse failing tasks plus a passing control. Current evidence does not justify a guessed temperature or cache fix.

No runtime, catalog, source or dependency fixes were made during this frozen comparison. The proposed work is separate from completion of this trial.

# Final coverage audit

**Complete: 258/258 unique planned cells, three repetitions for all 86 model/suite/scenario groups.** The three immutable journals contain 169 + 83 + 6 records. There were no retries or samples from the cancelled campaign. The final launcher exited 0 at 09:25 PDT, October 30; the 10:07 PDT process snapshot found no campaign or native processes.

## Review coverage

| Segment | Attempts | Artifact judgments | Cells judged | Missing artifact | No declared axes |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| original | 169 | 79 | 76 | 0 | 93 |
| continuation | 83 | 40 | 36 | 2 | 45 |
| final-six | 6 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 6 |

125 produced declared artifact paths map to 119 distinct contents and 119 judgments across 112 cells. Six identical copies share their content judgment. Two declared outputs are missing (Qwen week-plan r3 and Gemma refactor-module r3); they are noArtifact, not zero-valued judgments. The remaining 144 cells have no declared axes. All six final cells received diagnostic review without invented qualitative scores.

The independent audit checked each declared axis name, integer 0–10 scores, arithmetic mean, bounded review size (at most 20 KiB), artifact hash, provider/model metadata, and specific justification. Nine artifact judgments across six primary A/B cells have a documented HTML-rubric/Markdown-output mismatch; raw scores remain visible and applicable means exclude only those primary cells.

## Performance evidence across all attempts

| Metric | Available / 258 |
|---|---:|
| durationSeconds | 258/258 |
| firstActionSeconds | 257/258 |
| firstArtifactSeconds | 240/258 |
| toolCalls | 258/258 |

The final Gemma fanout attempt never started inference. Its raw HTTP counters are 0/0 in an unrelated anthropic-cli bucket; engine-derived local-model tokens are unavailable. The final analytical JSON/CSV correct this availability interpretation without changing raw metrics. Its memory/utilization samples describe the waiting daemon and ambient device, not loaded Gemma. First-artifact timings are 240/258; one Qwen large-PR write timing is documented separately in the continuation performance-supplement.json and does not overwrite the raw null.

## Identity and raw evidence

All 358 frozen source/build/catalog/native manifest files and six profile fingerprints matched at final verification. Both prior journal hashes are unchanged. The two no-OS-sandbox segments have byte-identical hooks and equal source/runtime/catalog/models/environment; campaign-local profile metadata differs. All expected per-trial result, score, facts, metrics, host and postmortem files exist, and every weighted fixed composite was recomputed successfully. Raw classifications and scores remain untouched: 256 raw-eligible records and two exclusions, plus one additional diagnostic admission issue.

## Early cross-cutting evidence

Both first-repetition petshop trials produced usable page markup but no requested raster logo. Completed facts show no generate_image call and a missing expected image-generator role. This is a role/tool coordination and recovery investigation; it is not evidence of unavailable native image inference. No additional task-failure retries were scheduled.

The two tank pages both passed the runtime gate. Source review distinguishes their depth: one implements lives, enemy fire, particles and restart; the other has iteration/removal risks and a barrel/shot orientation mismatch. Passing the gate is therefore insufficient evidence of product polish.

Visual-quality observations in this document are inferred from source. No extra rendered visual or interactive review has been performed.

# Continuation stopped at 252/258 — 2026-10-30 13:14 UTC

Parent: 169 records (168 aggregate-eligible). Continuation: 83 records (82 aggregate-eligible). Six original cells are unstarted. The two raw infrastructure exclusions are preserved.

- Qwen export/generalize ends after 2520.669 seconds and 74 calls: raw FAIL/3.8, failureClass infra, excluded from the model aggregate by gate-unevaluable. The terminal watchdog sees 305 seconds without model-turn progress after a recovery nudge. The classifier evidence is an earlier gate configuration error, not a Windows sandbox failure or a native launch failure.
- The model-authored supplier-quarter-intake template declares quarter but uses {{workPath}} without declaring a workPath default. On invocation quarter=q2 substitutes correctly; {{workPath}} remains literal in the first step gate. Two advance_task_step calls return gate_infrastructure_error and pause supplier-intake/2 before consuming a deliverable attempt. This is an invalid authored recipe plus an evaluation attribution limitation: failure-class.ts treats any unevaluable gate as infrastructure without distinguishing model-authored from fixture-owned gates. Preserve the raw exclusion; report the causal authoring evidence separately.
- Q1 runs through all three manual task steps to completion. Both final cleaned JSON arrays exactly match the six positive-lead-time source rows with every field preserved. Both final reports give correct eight/two/six totals and flagged names. Q2 flags were written to tasks/2/flags.md but the first recipe step never completes and publish never activates. The Q2 outputs exist outside that completed recipe path, so they do not demonstrate successful reusable orchestration. The Q2 flags note has a minor unsupported clean-minimum range endpoint: it says 190-520 while surviving minOrderValue spans 275-520.
- The terminal repair loop repeatedly queries how_do_i for craftbook repair documentation; replies return unrelated Plan, Brand Tone Rewrite, Automation Recipe, app-building, and Documentation Rewrite material. Logs show file-only scenario-repair mode while the remaining requirement is paused recipe/task state. This repeats the previously documented repair-surface mismatch. During inactivity the native engine repeatedly saves 31 context checkpoints (4638.411 MiB) plus about 203.415 MiB draft state. This corroborates cache activity, but does not prove what caused the stalled model turn.
- The behavior-zero prose-as-deliverable flag targets Reza's explicit progress update: Q1 is in progress, the saved recipe is authored, and Q2 is queued. The promised final files subsequently exist; this is another likely progress-message false positive. The recipe was authored before Q1 finished, weakening the intended do-once-then-generalize sequence. No new qualitative ratings are assigned because the scenario declares no judge axes.
- The continuation controller stopped after recording this infra classification and refuses restart when stopped is set. It exited with code 1 at 13:14:22 UTC; actual launcher, harness, daemon and native processes are gone. All 358 frozen source fingerprints, six profile files, service module, parent journal and clean commit still match. No stopped state was cleared, no attempt retried and no native payload or dependency changed.
